Hi Marguerite,

I had a similar coding debacle about a year ago that involved multiple levels of nesting and random and fixed effects (ugh!), but I think I finally figured it out using lme. 

Try this:

#your 'fence' effect is equivalent to your winter warming effect (main plot- I'm calling it WWWC), so you don't need to have both in your model
#I'm calling your summer warming trt (subplot) SCSW
#first line has all your fixed effects, second line specifies nesting structure of random effects

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW,
       data=data)


As far as data organization, I think that as long as your model is specified correctly, it doesn't matter much how you number your variables. Just have one column for each factor in your model, and make sure that R knows that everything is a factor.   

Hope that helps,
Emily

On Sun, Dec 7, 2014 at 10:07 PM, Marguerite Mauritz <mauritzm...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hello, 

I'm trying to analyse a blocked split plot design in lme4 and cannot figure out the correct code.

The design I have is a blocked split-plot design with repeated measures so I have 2 between-plot and 2 within-plot effects.
There are 3 random blocks on the landscape with two fences in each block. Each fence is split and has either a winter warming (WW) or no winter warming (WC). On either side of the fence there are 4 sub-plots, 2 of which have a summer warming treatment (SW) and 2 of which have no summer warming (SC). Every sub-plot is monitored once a year for 5 years. The question is whether carbon flux changes significantly between treatments and through time. 

It looks like this:

3 blocks replicated on the landscape, random between-subject effect 
2 fences nested in each block, this is the unit of replication for my fixed between-subject effect WW described below, these are coded 1-6 so that each fence in each block has a unique ID
1 treatment applied to each fence, either WW or WC, fixed between- subject effect
1 treatment crossed with each treatment at the fence level, either SW or SC, these are applied in 2 sub-plots per fence, fixed within-subject effect
this produces WWxSW, WWxSC, WCxSW and WCxSC treatments
each sub-plot is monitored once per year for 5 years, fixed within-subject effect

The tricky thing is that I want block/fence to be my unit of replication for the WW effect and I want sub-plot to be my unit of replication for years.

I want to make sure my variables are coded correctly. Currently each fence is unique 1:6, blocks are A,B,C and sub-plots are 1:8, repeated in every block/fence combination. This makes sense to me, the fences and blocks are unique; plot 1 in every block/fence comes from the same treatment and, if treatment has an effect, they should behave similarly regardless of where they are on the landscape.

I have a few model attempts, but I'm pretty sure they're all wrong. It's the different units of replication that are totally throwing me off.

# split-split plot design. I think this would be correct if WW and year had the same unit of replication?
model1 <- lmer(carbon ~ WW*SW*year +     
                 (1|block/fence/WW/year),
               data = d)

#  I don't think this is correct although it will run.
model2 <- lmer (carbon ~ WW*SW*year +               # these are my fixed effects, WW is between-subject and SW, year are within-subject
(1|block) +                                                        # random between-subject effect
(1+WW|block) + (1+WW|block:fence)             # I am not sure this is correct, I want it to be WW applied to fences nested in blocks
(1+year|sub-plot),                                             # also not sure this is right, I want it to be year repeated at the sub-plot level
data = d)

Every variation of model I have tried gives me 1 DF for each effect when I check the anova(model) output. That just doesn't make sense. Year should have 4. 

Part of the lmer output is a list of grouping variables after the random effects. 
summary(model1)

Number of obs: 240, groups:  
year:(WW:(fence:block)), 60; WW:(fence:block), 12; fence:block, 6; block, 3

What exactly do these mean? Are they the F-ratio denominator?

Thanks very much for any help,
Marguerite

parts:
Marguerite,

If I'm understanding your design correctly, you have fences (main plots) randomized within blocks, which is the same as saying you have WW nested in blocks. Then, you assigned two subplots to each main plot, which is the same as saying you nested SW within WW (or fence). Therefore, you could either use fences or WW in your model, and you could use subplots or WW, but I don't think you want to have both in your model.

Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1). 

Year is tricky, and where you should put it in your model probably depends on the purpose of taking measurements over time and what kind of inferences you want to make. For example, if you are really interested in the overall effect of each year, I could see putting it as your highest nesting factor (blocks nested in year, and so-on). But you said you want sub-plot to be your unit of replication for year, which means it would go at the end (i.e., year becomes a sort of 'sub-sub-plot'). So your model would look like this:

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW/year,
       data=data)

Then, I believe your DF for year should be 4 (5 years-1). 

You might want to consult with a statistician about what the appropriate degrees of freedom are for each factor given your design, and then make sure your model matches that. Knowing what the appropriate tests are for each factor gets tricky when you have a complicated design like this. Or perhaps someone with more experience in repeated measures designs could weigh in. 

Emily

On Monday, December 8, 2014 4:08:59 PM UTC-5, Emily Peffer wrote:
Marguerite,

If I'm understanding your design correctly, you have fences (main plots) randomized within blocks, which is the same as saying you have WW nested in blocks. Then, you assigned two subplots to each main plot, which is the same as saying you nested SW within WW (or fence). Therefore, you could either use fences or WW in your model, and you could use subplots or WW, but I don't think you want to have both in your model.

Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1). 

Year is tricky, and where you should put it in your model probably depends on the purpose of taking measurements over time and what kind of inferences you want to make. For example, if you are really interested in the overall effect of each year, I could see putting it as your highest nesting factor (blocks nested in year, and so-on). But you said you want sub-plot to be your unit of replication for year, which means it would go at the end (i.e., year becomes a sort of 'sub-sub-plot'). So your model would look like this:

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW/year,
       data=data)

Then, I believe your DF for year should be 4 (5 years-1). 

You might want to consult with a statistician about what the appropriate degrees of freedom are for each factor given your design, and then make sure your model matches that. Knowing what the appropriate tests are for each factor gets tricky when you have a complicated design like this. Or perhaps someone with more experience in repeated measures designs could weigh in. 

Emily

I had a similar coding debacle about a year ago that involved multiple levels of nesting and random and fixed effects (ugh!), but I think I finally figured it out using lme. 

Try this:

#I'm calling your summer warming trt (subplot) SCSW

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW,
       data=data)


As far as data organization, I think that as long as your model is specified correctly, it doesn't matter much how you number your variables. Just have one column for each factor in your model, and make sure that R knows that everything is a factor.   

Hope that helps,
Emily

Just to confirm- each fence has only one WW treatment, right? So each block has two different WW treatments? If so, fence is your experimental unit for WW. You are not really interested in the effect of fence, correct? The reason to include block in the model is because you randomized WW treatments within block (2 fences, one treatment per fence). Therefore, some of the error within your treatments may be attributable to areas on the landscape, and you want to reduce this source of error. But I still don't see why you would include fence. The way the model that includes fence in your last email is set up, it's saying your WW treatment is nested in fence, which is nested in block. But WW is not really nested in fence if there's only one treatment applied to the fence. If you didn't have a WW treatment, and only had a SW treatment, then your SW would be nested in fence, because there are two treatments per fence. Unless I am misunderstanding your design. 

I think the error in your last model is because you include fence and sub-plot.  If you look at your "Number of groups", the numbers within each group are inflated.

I think it's okay to use anova() for the lme output. One thing to be aware of is that it uses Type I (sequential) sums of squares. There's a big debate about which type of SS is most appropriate for different designs and goals, but the conclusion I came to was that Type I was best for nested designs. 

Hopefully a statistician, or someone on this listserv with more statistical prowess, can help confirm how to appropriately specify your model. Let me know what you end up with, I'm curious! 

Emily

Marguerite,

If I'm understanding your design correctly, you have fences (main plots) randomized within blocks, which is the same as saying you have WW nested in blocks. Then, you assigned two subplots to each main plot, which is the same as saying you nested SW within WW (or fence). Therefore, you could either use fences or WW in your model, and you could use subplots or WW, but I don't think you want to have both in your model.

Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1). 

Year is tricky, and where you should put it in your model probably depends on the purpose of taking measurements over time and what kind of inferences you want to make. For example, if you are really interested in the overall effect of each year, I could see putting it as your highest nesting factor (blocks nested in year, and so-on). But you said you want sub-plot to be your unit of replication for year, which means it would go at the end (i.e., year becomes a sort of 'sub-sub-plot'). So your model would look like this:

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW/year,
       data=data)

Then, I believe your DF for year should be 4 (5 years-1). 

You might want to consult with a statistician about what the appropriate degrees of freedom are for each factor given your design, and then make sure your model matches that. Knowing what the appropriate tests are for each factor gets tricky when you have a complicated design like this. Or perhaps someone with more experience in repeated measures designs could weigh in. 

Emily

Marguerite,

If I'm understanding your design correctly, you have fences (main plots) randomized within blocks, which is the same as saying you have WW nested in blocks. Then, you assigned two subplots to each main plot, which is the same as saying you nested SW within WW (or fence). Therefore, you could either use fences or WW in your model, and you could use subplots or WW, but I don't think you want to have both in your model.

Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1). 

Year is tricky, and where you should put it in your model probably depends on the purpose of taking measurements over time and what kind of inferences you want to make. For example, if you are really interested in the overall effect of each year, I could see putting it as your highest nesting factor (blocks nested in year, and so-on). But you said you want sub-plot to be your unit of replication for year, which means it would go at the end (i.e., year becomes a sort of 'sub-sub-plot'). So your model would look like this:

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW/year,
       data=data)

Then, I believe your DF for year should be 4 (5 years-1). 

You might want to consult with a statistician about what the appropriate degrees of freedom are for each factor given your design, and then make sure your model matches that. Knowing what the appropriate tests are for each factor gets tricky when you have a complicated design like this. Or perhaps someone with more experience in repeated measures designs could weigh in.

Marguerite,

If I'm understanding your design correctly, you have fences (main plots) randomized within blocks, which is the same as saying you have WW nested in blocks. Then, you assigned two subplots to each main plot, which is the same as saying you nested SW within WW (or fence). Therefore, you could either use fences or WW in your model, and you could use subplots or WW, but I don't think you want to have both in your model.

Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1). 

Year is tricky, and where you should put it in your model probably depends on the purpose of taking measurements over time and what kind of inferences you want to make. For example, if you are really interested in the overall effect of each year, I could see putting it as your highest nesting factor (blocks nested in year, and so-on). But you said you want sub-plot to be your unit of replication for year, which means it would go at the end (i.e., year becomes a sort of 'sub-sub-plot'). So your model would look like this:

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW/year,
       data=data)

Then, I believe your DF for year should be 4 (5 years-1). 

You might want to consult with a statistician about what the appropriate degrees of freedom are for each factor given your design, and then make sure your model matches that. Knowing what the appropriate tests are for each factor gets tricky when you have a complicated design like this. Or perhaps someone with more experience in repeated measures designs could weigh in.

Marguerite,

If I'm understanding your design correctly, you have fences (main plots) randomized within blocks, which is the same as saying you have WW nested in blocks. Then, you assigned two subplots to each main plot, which is the same as saying you nested SW within WW (or fence). Therefore, you could either use fences or WW in your model, and you could use subplots or WW, but I don't think you want to have both in your model.

Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1). 

Year is tricky, and where you should put it in your model probably depends on the purpose of taking measurements over time and what kind of inferences you want to make. For example, if you are really interested in the overall effect of each year, I could see putting it as your highest nesting factor (blocks nested in year, and so-on). But you said you want sub-plot to be your unit of replication for year, which means it would go at the end (i.e., year becomes a sort of 'sub-sub-plot'). So your model would look like this:

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW/year,
       data=data)

Then, I believe your DF for year should be 4 (5 years-1). 

You might want to consult with a statistician about what the appropriate degrees of freedom are for each factor given your design, and then make sure your model matches that. Knowing what the appropriate tests are for each factor gets tricky when you have a complicated design like this. Or perhaps someone with more experience in repeated measures designs could weigh in. 

Emily

Marguerite,

If I'm understanding your design correctly, you have fences (main plots) randomized within blocks, which is the same as saying you have WW nested in blocks. Then, you assigned two subplots to each main plot, which is the same as saying you nested SW within WW (or fence). Therefore, you could either use fences or WW in your model, and you could use subplots or WW, but I don't think you want to have both in your model.

Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1). 

Year is tricky, and where you should put it in your model probably depends on the purpose of taking measurements over time and what kind of inferences you want to make. For example, if you are really interested in the overall effect of each year, I could see putting it as your highest nesting factor (blocks nested in year, and so-on). But you said you want sub-plot to be your unit of replication for year, which means it would go at the end (i.e., year becomes a sort of 'sub-sub-plot'). So your model would look like this:

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW/year,
       data=data)

Then, I believe your DF for year should be 4 (5 years-1). 

You might want to consult with a statistician about what the appropriate degrees of freedom are for each factor given your design, and then make sure your model matches that. Knowing what the appropriate tests are for each factor gets tricky when you have a complicated design like this. Or perhaps someone with more experience in repeated measures designs could weigh in. 

Emily

Marguerite,

If I'm understanding your design correctly, you have fences (main plots) randomized within blocks, which is the same as saying you have WW nested in blocks. Then, you assigned two subplots to each main plot, which is the same as saying you nested SW within WW (or fence). Therefore, you could either use fences or WW in your model, and you could use subplots or WW, but I don't think you want to have both in your model.

Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1). 

Year is tricky, and where you should put it in your model probably depends on the purpose of taking measurements over time and what kind of inferences you want to make. For example, if you are really interested in the overall effect of each year, I could see putting it as your highest nesting factor (blocks nested in year, and so-on). But you said you want sub-plot to be your unit of replication for year, which means it would go at the end (i.e., year becomes a sort of 'sub-sub-plot'). So your model would look like this:

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW/year,
       data=data)

Then, I believe your DF for year should be 4 (5 years-1). 

You might want to consult with a statistician about what the appropriate degrees of freedom are for each factor given your design, and then make sure your model matches that. Knowing what the appropriate tests are for each factor gets tricky when you have a complicated design like this. Or perhaps someone with more experience in repeated measures designs could weigh in. 

Emily

Hi Marguerite, 

Sorry for the delay in responding. Thanks for providing the details. 

With the disclaimer that I Am Not a Statistician, without randomization of whole plot factors to whole plots (fence sides) and split-plot factors to subplots, the assumptions of a split-plot design aren't met. In your case the first randomization maybe isn't too meaningful (ie maybe the fence orientations are already random), but the second seems important and lacking in the design you're analyzing. Talking to a statistician seems like a good idea, but be prepared for a bad response given the lack of randomization!

If the assumptions WERE met, specification of a split plot follows Pinheiro/Bates Oats example (see section 1.6 of their book, or the code available here https://www.stat.wisc.edu/courses/st850-lindstro/handouts/splitplotlme.pdf) Your example would have some differences. Below is my understanding of how they would work in nlme/lmer

- In Oats each treatment of the split plot factor is only applied to one subplot, while in your case there are two, this introduces another level of nesting at the (physical) spilt plot level.  Specifying this in the Oats example would be redundant to the fixed effects on nitro (something like yield ~  Variety * ordered(nitro) + (1 | Block/Variety/nitro) which causes an error because there's one Block:Variety:nitro level for each observation!)

- Your repeated measures, which are also part of the question (is there a change over time?). Specifying RE at the subplot level will also take care of this, with no need to year in the RE term. Adding year will make the model saturated. m_simple below implements this (and is the same as Emily's suggestion but without Year as the final level of RE). Simply specifying within-subplot RE doesn't formally account for temporal autocorrelation within subplot -- to do that see ?nlme::corAR1). First just look at random slope on year (see below). I think this is the best option and if the within-subplot residuals look ok corAR1 isn't necessary.

- Fences within Blocks: this is worth trying to account for but there may not be the data to estimate it

 
# Questions: whether carbon flux changes significantly between treatments and through time. 

# make unique variables for each nested unit
# this makes sthings clearer to you and 
# if you use lme4 it will then recognize the implicit nesting 
data <- within(data, {
    wholeplot <- factor(block:fence:WW)
    subplot <- factor(block:fence:WW:SW)
})

m_simple <- lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year, 
       random= ~ 1 |fence/wholeplot/subplot,
       data=data)

## this (or analogous version accounting for block) makes most sense as it allows for with subplot differences in response and could be implemented in lme or lmer
## it seems necessary if data show variation in temporal trend within WWWC:SCSW combinations but the fit may be unhealthy (very high correlation between slope and intercept within subplot)
## 
m_rs <-  lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year, 
       random= ~ 1 + year |fence/wholeplot/subplot,
       data=data)

## there are only 3 blocks and 6 fences per block so unlikely to be able to estimate this fully hierarchical specification of the RE
m_hier <- lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year, 
       random= ~ 1 |block/fence/wholeplot/subplot,
       data=data)

## equivalent in lme4 -- can do all of above but no corAR1 
detach(package:nlme)
library(lme4)

m_simple_lmer <- lmer(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year + (1 |fence/wholeplot/subplot),
       data=data)

Marguerite,

If I'm understanding your design correctly, you have fences (main plots) randomized within blocks, which is the same as saying you have WW nested in blocks. Then, you assigned two subplots to each main plot, which is the same as saying you nested SW within WW (or fence). Therefore, you could either use fences or WW in your model, and you could use subplots or WW, but I don't think you want to have both in your model.

Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1). 

Year is tricky, and where you should put it in your model probably depends on the purpose of taking measurements over time and what kind of inferences you want to make. For example, if you are really interested in the overall effect of each year, I could see putting it as your highest nesting factor (blocks nested in year, and so-on). But you said you want sub-plot to be your unit of replication for year, which means it would go at the end (i.e., year becomes a sort of 'sub-sub-plot'). So your model would look like this:

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW/year,
       data=data)

Then, I believe your DF for year should be 4 (5 years-1). 

You might want to consult with a statistician about what the appropriate degrees of freedom are for each factor given your design, and then make sure your model matches that. Knowing what the appropriate tests are for each factor gets tricky when you have a complicated design like this. Or perhaps someone with more experience in repeated measures designs could weigh in. 

Emily

On Thursday, December 11, 2014 2:25:27 PM UTC-5, Jaime Ashander wrote:
Hi Marguerite, 

Sorry for the delay in responding. Thanks for providing the details. 

With the disclaimer that I Am Not a Statistician, without randomization of whole plot factors to whole plots (fence sides) and split-plot factors to subplots, the assumptions of a split-plot design aren't met. In your case the first randomization maybe isn't too meaningful (ie maybe the fence orientations are already random), but the second seems important and lacking in the design you're analyzing. Talking to a statistician seems like a good idea, but be prepared for a bad response given the lack of randomization!

If the assumptions WERE met, specification of a split plot follows Pinheiro/Bates Oats example (see section 1.6 of their book, or the code available here https://www.stat.wisc.edu/courses/st850-lindstro/handouts/splitplotlme.pdf) Your example would have some differences. Below is my understanding of how they would work in nlme/lmer

- In Oats each treatment of the split plot factor is only applied to one subplot, while in your case there are two, this introduces another level of nesting at the (physical) spilt plot level.  Specifying this in the Oats example would be redundant to the fixed effects on nitro (something like yield ~  Variety * ordered(nitro) + (1 | Block/Variety/nitro) which causes an error because there's one Block:Variety:nitro level for each observation!)

- Your repeated measures, which are also part of the question (is there a change over time?). Specifying RE at the subplot level will also take care of this, with no need to year in the RE term. Adding year will make the model saturated. m_simple below implements this (and is the same as Emily's suggestion but without Year as the final level of RE). Simply specifying within-subplot RE doesn't formally account for temporal autocorrelation within subplot -- to do that see ?nlme::corAR1). First just look at random slope on year (see below). I think this is the best option and if the within-subplot residuals look ok corAR1 isn't necessary.

- Fences within Blocks: this is worth trying to account for but there may not be the data to estimate it

 
# Questions: whether carbon flux changes significantly between treatments and through time. 

# make unique variables for each nested unit
# this makes sthings clearer to you and 
# if you use lme4 it will then recognize the implicit nesting 
data <- within(data, {
    wholeplot <- factor(block:fence:WW)
    subplot <- factor(block:fence:WW:SW)
})

If I'm understanding your design correctly, you have fences (main plots) randomized within blocks, which is the same as saying you have WW nested in blocks. Then, you assigned two subplots to each main plot, which is the same as saying you nested SW within WW (or fence). Therefore, you could either use fences or WW in your model, and you could use subplots or WW, but I don't think you want to have both in your model.

Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1). 

Year is tricky, and where you should put it in your model probably depends on the purpose of taking measurements over time and what kind of inferences you want to make. For example, if you are really interested in the overall effect of each year, I could see putting it as your highest nesting factor (blocks nested in year, and so-on). But you said you want sub-plot to be your unit of replication for year, which means it would go at the end (i.e., year becomes a sort of 'sub-sub-plot'). So your model would look like this:

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW/year,
       data=data)

Then, I believe your DF for year should be 4 (5 years-1). 

You might want to consult with a statistician about what the appropriate degrees of freedom are for each factor given your design, and then make sure your model matches that. Knowing what the appropriate tests are for each factor gets tricky when you have a complicated design like this. Or perhaps someone with more experience in repeated measures designs could weigh in.

Hi Marguerite, 

Sorry for the delay in responding. Thanks for providing the details. 

With the disclaimer that I Am Not a Statistician, without randomization of whole plot factors to whole plots (fence sides) and split-plot factors to subplots, the assumptions of a split-plot design aren't met. In your case the first randomization maybe isn't too meaningful (ie maybe the fence orientations are already random), but the second seems important and lacking in the design you're analyzing. Talking to a statistician seems like a good idea, but be prepared for a bad response given the lack of randomization!

If the assumptions WERE met, specification of a split plot follows Pinheiro/Bates Oats example (see section 1.6 of their book, or the code available here https://www.stat.wisc.edu/courses/st850-lindstro/handouts/splitplotlme.pdf) Your example would have some differences. Below is my understanding of how they would work in nlme/lmer

- In Oats each treatment of the split plot factor is only applied to one subplot, while in your case there are two, this introduces another level of nesting at the (physical) spilt plot level.  Specifying this in the Oats example would be redundant to the fixed effects on nitro (something like yield ~  Variety * ordered(nitro) + (1 | Block/Variety/nitro) which causes an error because there's one Block:Variety:nitro level for each observation!)

- Your repeated measures, which are also part of the question (is there a change over time?). Specifying RE at the subplot level will also take care of this, with no need to year in the RE term. Adding year will make the model saturated. m_simple below implements this (and is the same as Emily's suggestion but without Year as the final level of RE). Simply specifying within-subplot RE doesn't formally account for temporal autocorrelation within subplot -- to do that see ?nlme::corAR1). First just look at random slope on year (see below). I think this is the best option and if the within-subplot residuals look ok corAR1 isn't necessary.

- Fences within Blocks: this is worth trying to account for but there may not be the data to estimate it

 
# Questions: whether carbon flux changes significantly between treatments and through time.

# this makes sthings clearer to you and 
# if you use lme4 it will then recognize the implicit nesting 
data <- within(data, {
    wholeplot <- factor(block:fence:WW)
    subplot <- factor(block:fence:WW:SW)
})

m_simple <- lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year, 
       random= ~ 1 |fence/wholeplot/subplot,
       data=data)

Marguerite,

If I'm understanding your design correctly, you have fences (main plots) randomized within blocks, which is the same as saying you have WW nested in blocks. Then, you assigned two subplots to each main plot, which is the same as saying you nested SW within WW (or fence). Therefore, you could either use fences or WW in your model, and you could use subplots or WW, but I don't think you want to have both in your model.

Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1). 

Year is tricky, and where you should put it in your model probably depends on the purpose of taking measurements over time and what kind of inferences you want to make. For example, if you are really interested in the overall effect of each year, I could see putting it as your highest nesting factor (blocks nested in year, and so-on). But you said you want sub-plot to be your unit of replication for year, which means it would go at the end (i.e., year becomes a sort of 'sub-sub-plot'). So your model would look like this:

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW/year,
       data=data)

Then, I believe your DF for year should be 4 (5 years-1). 

You might want to consult with a statistician about what the appropriate degrees of freedom are for each factor given your design, and then make sure your model matches that. Knowing what the appropriate tests are for each factor gets tricky when you have a complicated design like this. Or perhaps someone with more experience in repeated measures designs could weigh in.

Hi Marguerite, 

Sorry for the delay in responding. Thanks for providing the details. 

With the disclaimer that I Am Not a Statistician, without randomization of whole plot factors to whole plots (fence sides) and split-plot factors to subplots, the assumptions of a split-plot design aren't met. In your case the first randomization maybe isn't too meaningful (ie maybe the fence orientations are already random), but the second seems important and lacking in the design you're analyzing. Talking to a statistician seems like a good idea, but be prepared for a bad response given the lack of randomization!

If the assumptions WERE met, specification of a split plot follows Pinheiro/Bates Oats example (see section 1.6 of their book, or the code available here https://www.stat.wisc.edu/courses/st850-lindstro/handouts/splitplotlme.pdf) Your example would have some differences. Below is my understanding of how they would work in nlme/lmer

- In Oats each treatment of the split plot factor is only applied to one subplot, while in your case there are two, this introduces another level of nesting at the (physical) spilt plot level.  Specifying this in the Oats example would be redundant to the fixed effects on nitro (something like yield ~  Variety * ordered(nitro) + (1 | Block/Variety/nitro) which causes an error because there's one Block:Variety:nitro level for each observation!)

- Your repeated measures, which are also part of the question (is there a change over time?). Specifying RE at the subplot level will also take care of this, with no need to year in the RE term. Adding year will make the model saturated. m_simple below implements this (and is the same as Emily's suggestion but without Year as the final level of RE). Simply specifying within-subplot RE doesn't formally account for temporal autocorrelation within subplot -- to do that see ?nlme::corAR1). First just look at random slope on year (see below). I think this is the best option and if the within-subplot residuals look ok corAR1 isn't necessary.

- Fences within Blocks: this is worth trying to account for but there may not be the data to estimate it

 
# Questions: whether carbon flux changes significantly between treatments and through time. 

# make unique variables for each nested unit
# this makes sthings clearer to you and 
# if you use lme4 it will then recognize the implicit nesting 
data <- within(data, {
    wholeplot <- factor(block:fence:WW)
    subplot <- factor(block:fence:WW:SW)
})

m_simple <- lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year, 
       random= ~ 1 |fence/wholeplot/subplot,
       data=data)

## this (or analogous version accounting for block) makes most sense as it allows for with subplot differences in response and could be implemented in lme or lmer
## it seems necessary if data show variation in temporal trend within WWWC:SCSW combinations but the fit may be unhealthy (very high correlation between slope and intercept within subplot)
## 
m_rs <-  lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year, 
       random= ~ 1 + year |fence/wholeplot/subplot,
       data=data)

## there are only 3 blocks and 6 fences per block so unlikely to be able to estimate this fully hierarchical specification of the RE
m_hier <- lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year, 
       random= ~ 1 |block/fence/wholeplot/subplot,
       data=data)

## equivalent in lme4 -- can do all of above but no corAR1 
detach(package:nlme)
library(lme4)

m_simple_lmer <- lmer(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year + (1 |fence/wholeplot/subplot),

If I'm understanding your design correctly, you have fences (main plots) randomized within blocks, which is the same as saying you have WW nested in blocks. Then, you assigned two subplots to each main plot, which is the same as saying you nested SW within WW (or fence). Therefore, you could either use fences or WW in your model, and you could use subplots or WW, but I don't think you want to have both in your model.

Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1). 

Year is tricky, and where you should put it in your model probably depends on the purpose of taking measurements over time and what kind of inferences you want to make. For example, if you are really interested in the overall effect of each year, I could see putting it as your highest nesting factor (blocks nested in year, and so-on). But you said you want sub-plot to be your unit of replication for year, which means it would go at the end (i.e., year becomes a sort of 'sub-sub-plot'). So your model would look like this:

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW/year,
       data=data)

Then, I believe your DF for year should be 4 (5 years-1). 

You might want to consult with a statistician about what the appropriate degrees of freedom are for each factor given your design, and then make sure your model matches that. Knowing what the appropriate tests are for each factor gets tricky when you have a complicated design like this. Or perhaps someone with more experience in repeated measures designs could weigh in.

Hi, 

I have been extremely remiss in posting a response to outline the final model that I have ended up with. I apologise, but better late than not at all, since I hope others find this thread useful. 
After the helpful advice I received here, some reading, and discussion with a statistician here at Northern Arizona University, I came up with the following analytic approach: 

I first have to define an explicit nesting structure, to be certain that lme4 can recognise the sample design. I then put the split-plot block design structure in the random effects, allowing for random intercepts. The random effect structure was not tested for significance (or explanatory power) because it is an integral part of the experimental design and therefore should not be excluded, even if the random effect offers no model improvement. In the summary output I can look at the variance associated with each random component, in order to understand where most of the variation lies. 
In order to account for the repeated measures aspect of the experiment I include a categorical year effect in the random effects, and allow the intercept to be different in each year of the study. This allows the 'starting point' of each year to be different. The effect of change through time is tested by including a continuous time variable, centered on 0, in the fixed effects. This tests whether the slope through time is significant. Centering the variable is useful because it constrains the model to the time interval over which I have data; I do not want 2009-2013 as real numeric values, since that makes no sense. My starting year is 2009, not calendar year 0. 
The other fixed effects are treatments, I set a reference for each treatment, to make sure that the model intercepts represent the 'control' treatment. By allowing full interactions: WW*SW*time I am able to represent the crossed nature of the WW*SW treatment and can test whether the changes through time differ with treatments. 

Finally, I can look at the summary output of the model, calculate confidence intervals for the fixed effects (not-overlapping zero is significant at the 95% CI), and determine residuals of the fixed and random effects.

Code below: 
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
library(lme4)
library(sjPlot)

# Prepare the data for stats
# data that contains the CO2 flux (NEE.sum) dependent response variables, and independent predictor variables: WW, SW, and WW x SW treatment, years that the experiment ran

data2 <- flux.variables 

# make unique variables for each nested unit for clarity, lme4 will recognise the implicit nesting
data2$block <- as.factor(data2$block)

# make model with fence coded 1-2 and plot coded 1-4, then create unique names for each fence, WW or plot
data2$fence_2 <- ifelse(data2$fence == 1 | data2$fence == 3 | data2$fence == 5, "1", "2") 
data2$plot_4 <- ifelse(data2$plot == 1 | data2$plot == 5, "1",
                       ifelse(data2$plot == 2 | data2$plot == 6, "2",
                              ifelse(data2$plot == 3 | data2$plot == 7, "3","4")))


data2$fence_2 <- as.factor(data2$fence_2)
data2$plot <- as.factor(data2$plot)
data2$plot_4 <- as.factor(data2$plot_4)

# create variable for random structure
data2 <- within (data2, {
  wholeplot <- factor(block:fence_2:WW)
  SWplot <- factor(block:fence_2:WW:SW) # this is in case I want to nest SW
  subplot4 <- factor(block:fence_2:WW:plot_4)
})

# stats lab consultation with Derek Sonderegger:
# For repeated measures
# make time a continuous variable to put in main effects (to test year effect) 
# and make year a categorical variable and include in random effects

# center time on 0 so that 2009 is used as the reference year
baseyear <- min(data2$year)
data2$time <- as.numeric(data2$year - baseyear)

# make year a factor:
# categorical variable to put in random structure (time will be continuous as fixed effect),
# year effect will account for the offset from the overall trend throught time
data2$year <- as.factor(data2$year)

# reorder levels of time and treatment in the data to make sure that control in year 2009 is the reference
# for the intercept
print(levels(data2$treatment))
print(levels(factor(data2$time)))

data2$treatment <- relevel(data2$treatment, ref="Control")
print(levels(data2$treatment))

# The data look like this: 
 year fence  treatment block SW WW    NEE.sum      fence_2  plot_4      subplot4  SWplot       wholeplot    time
1: 2009     1        Air        A      S  C        -29.318239       1            1            A:1:C:1     A:1:C:S     A:1:C          0

4: 2009     1    Control     A     C  C        3.516462         1             4        A:1:C:4          A:1:C:C     A:1:C          0
5: 2009     1 Air & Soil    A      S  W      -13.604757       1             1        A:1:W:1        A:1:W:S     A:1:W         0

# Model1:
# WW * SW * time: effects of treatment over time;
# WW is nested and SW is crossed (split-plot design);
# WW is part of the random nesting structure;
# whole plot is: block/fence/WW;

model1 <- lmer(NEE.sum ~ WW * SW * time + # use * or + depending on the interactions you want to specify
                 (1 | block/fence_2/wholeplot/subplot4) + (1|year), 
               data = data2)

# display output of model and the effect size of each fixed effect
summary(model1)
# display the confidence interval around each fixed effect
confint(model1,method="boot",boot.type="norm",level=0.95,nsim=1000)

# I also want to know whether the distribution of residuals and model fit differ
# between the model with time and the model with environmental/biological predictors.
model1resids <- resid(model1)
model1fitted <- fitted(model1)
model1sqrtres <- sqrt(abs(resid(model1)))

par(mfrow=c(2,2), mar = c(4,4,3,2))
plot(model1fitted, model1resids, main='resid, model1: WW*SW*time')
plot(model1fitted, model1sqrtres, main='sqrt resid, model1: WW*SW*time')

# I believe that this will apply to all models with the same response variable since
# the RE structure remains the same.

sjp.glmer(model1, type="re.qq")

#your 'fence' effect is equivalent to your winter warming effect (main plot- I'm calling it WWWC), so you don't need to have both in your model
#I'm calling your summer warming trt (subplot) SCSW
#first line has all your fixed effects, second line specifies nesting structure of random effects

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW, 
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW,
       data=data)


As far as data organization, I think that as long as your model is specified correctly, it doesn't matter much how you number your variables. Just have one column for each factor in your model, and make sure that R knows that everything is a factor.   

Hope that helps,
Emily
